query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated, active‐learning machine‐learning potential (MLP) framework calibrated with a minimal set of ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) data can generate accurate free energy surfaces for both solid and liquid phases—accounting for vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling—with a computational cost reduced by at least one order of magnitude relative to explicit AIMD (and TOR-TILD) calculations.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, or multicomponent high‐entropy systems in both their crystalline (solid) and disordered (liquid) configurations near the melting point.
generation.intervention: Deploy an active-learning MLP (e.g., deep potential or moment tensor potential) that is iteratively trained on a sparse but strategically enhanced AIMD dataset. Then, use this MLP in conjunction with a free-energy integration method (e.g., Gaussian process–aided thermodynamic integration similar to TOR-TILD) to compute the free energy differences and entropy contributions of both phases.
generation.conditions: The method should be applied in temperature regimes near fusion where both solid and liquid free energies are needed. It is expected to work for systems where the high-dimensional configuration space is adequately sampled by active learning, including multicomponent and high-entropy alloys, provided that the anharmonic contributions are moderate and the relevant electronic contributions are captured in the training data.
generation.structural_mediator: The MLP serves as the mediator by encoding the interatomic forces and energies, thereby implicitly reproducing the key vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration couplings observed in AIMD simulations without needing exhaustive sampling.
generation.mechanism: By replacing the expensive on-the-fly evaluation of forces and energies in AIMD with a surrogate model calibrated via active learning, the computational cost per time step is drastically reduced. Simultaneously, the free energy integration (augmented by uncertainty-aware Gaussian process regression) efficiently accumulates the necessary entropy contributions. This dual approach preserves the fidelity of the phase free energy evaluations while overcoming the scaling bottleneck of traditional methods.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion free energies, melting temperatures, and high-temperature thermodynamic properties calculated via the MLP framework will closely match those from explicit AIMD/TOR-TILD methods (within an acceptable error margin, e.g., <10%), but with a reduction in computation time by at least a factor of 10.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio free-energy integration via AIMD and TOR-TILD for both solid and liquid states.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be most effective when the training dataset covers the relevant configurational space of both phases and the anharmonic effects remain within the range learned by the MLP. Extreme cases with very strong anharmonicity or highly localized electron–phonon couplings may require further refinement or additional training data.
generation.uncertainty: The precise amount of AIMD sampling needed to cover the necessary phase space and the degree to which subtle electronic contributions (e.g., electron–vibration coupling) are captured remain to be quantified. Additionally, the transferability of the trained MLP across different compositions (especially in complex high-entropy systems) is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative multicomponent system (e.g., a refractory high-entropy alloy) near its melting point. First, compute the free energies of its solid and liquid phases using explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD. Next, develop an MLP using an active learning protocol with a limited AIMD training set and compute the same free energies via the MLP-based free-energy integration. Compare both sets of results and record the computational cost and accuracy.
measurements: Free energy values of the solid and liquid phases
Total computational time and resource usage
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if (a) the MLP-based method yields free energy differences, melting temperatures, or vibrational entropy values that deviate by more than approximately 10% from those obtained by explicit AIMD/TOR-TILD, or (b) the computational cost reduction is less than one order of magnitude compared to the baseline methods.

cited_evidence.text: Additionally, free energy corrections to the PES barrier can be computed. These rely on calculating the vibrational modes of the reactants in the initial, final, and transition state configurations and are thus somewhat more involved. Most commonly, the harmonic approximation (HA) is used in this context, meaning that a second-order Taylor expansion of the PES around the configurations of interest is performed, from which the finite-temperature free energy corrections can be calculated analytically. While applying the HA is relatively straightforward in principle, it is known to be inadequate at higher temperatures and for low-frequency modes, such as hindered translations or rotations., These factors lead to some ambiguity on how to treat (or whether to neglect) slow modes and overall add to the uncertainty of predicted free energy barriers. Fortunately, the success of machine-learning (ML) interatomic potentials in chemistry and materials science in recent years has opened a new perspective for free energy calculations in heterogeneous catalysis. Machine learning techniques are increasingly used to bypass expensive quantum chemical computations. Typical examples are machine learning-based potentials that are exploited to propagate the dynamical evolution of molecular systems on ab initio potentials at a fraction of the cost. The seminal work in the field comes from Behler and Parrinello, who trained a generalized Artificial Neural Network (ANN) capable of predicting density functional theory-based energies and atomic forces and demonstrated its capability on bulk silicon and then on carbon, and sodium. Behler and Marquetand then applied the same approach to n-alkanes and alanine tripeptides. Comparable capabilities were achieved by Csanyi and co-workers, who used kernel-based method (i.e., the Gaussian approximation potential) to propagate the density functional theory (DFT)–molecular dynamics (MD) of bulk crystal, amorphous carbon, and silicon. Kernel ridge methods were also exploited for the “on-the-fly” propagation of the dynamic in the electronic states, circumventing the need for the explicit time dependent DFT or the CASSCF computations. The method applies generally to solids, but the particular implementation given here relies on the accuracy of a Gaussian approximation to the distribution function. Hence it is most likely to work when the atomic displacements are small, and it is likely to fail in molecular solids where coherent bond rotations are present. Although we mainly demonstrated the method for elemental solids, it also holds in principle for complex crystalline and noncrystalline solids. We give an example of such an application for the MoNbTaW high entropy alloy. The quasiharmonic method may be equally accurate and more efficient than our AIMD method when anharmonicity mainly enters through thermal expansion, but a simulation-based approach in principle includes additional anharmonic contributions. Doing so may require correlations beyond those captured by the Gaussian approximation (see Section 3.3.1). Our simulation-based approach seems most useful when the simulation has already been completed for other purposes. Then, the entropy comes essentially for free on top of whatever other information was sought.
